messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kofi had always taken pride in his work as a bomb disposal technician. He had spent decades honing his skills and saving countless lives. But everything changed on that fateful day when he was exposed to toxic chemicals during a routine operation. The smell of antiseptic and the sounds of the hospital where he was treated still haunted him. As Kofi returned to work, he found himself becoming increasingly anxious in the workplace. He would catch himself scanning his surroundings for signs of danger, searching for escape routes before feeling comfortable anywhere. Loud noises, once a normal part of his job, now made him jump with alarm. His colleagues noticed the change in him and grew concerned. Kofi tried to brush it off, but he couldn't shake the feeling that he was constantly on edge. To cope with these feelings, Kofi started working excessively long hours, using the excuse that he needed to stay focused on his work. In reality, he was trying to avoid being alone with his thoughts. He would often volunteer for extra shifts or take on additional projects, just so he wouldn't have to go home and face the silence of his own company. His wife, Ama, noticed the change in him and tried to talk to him about it, but Kofi just shrugged it off, saying he was fine. As time went on, Kofi's avoidance behaviors only intensified. He started avoiding hospitals and ambulances, even going so far as to take detours to avoid driving past them. The smell of antiseptic would transport him back to that hospital room, and he couldn't bear the memories that came flooding back. His colleagues began to notice his absences from training exercises and team meetings, but Kofi just said he was "taking care of some personal stuff." Despite his efforts to avoid triggers, Kofi found himself constantly on high alert. He would react with alarm when someone touched him unexpectedly, and his eyes would scan the room for potential dangers. His wife started to feel like she was walking on eggshells around him, never knowing what might set him off. Ama tried to be patient, but it was taking a toll on their relationship. Kofi knew he needed help, but he was afraid of facing his demons. He was certain that if he stopped working so much, the memories would come flooding back, and he wouldn't be able to cope. He felt like he was trapped in a never-ending cycle of fear and avoidance, with no escape route in sight. It wasn't until Kofi had a close call on the job, when a loud noise sent him running for cover, that he realized he needed help. His colleagues staged an intervention, telling him they couldn't keep working with someone who was so clearly struggling. Ama sat him down and told him she loved him, but she couldn't watch him destroy himself anymore. Kofi finally broke down, admitting that he had been living in a constant state of fear since the accident. He was afraid of losing his job, his marriage, and even himself. With tears streaming down his face, he asked for help, hoping to find a way out of the cycle of terror that had consumed him.
